analysis_steps.goal: Construct stellar mass surface density maps from VLT MUSE cubes

method.value: Correct MUSE mosaics for Milky Way extinction, Voronoi bin to S/N ~ 35 in 5300-5500 A, fit SSP templates in 4850-7000 A using pPXF within the PHANGS-MUSE DAP, reconstruct stellar mass maps from template weights, and mask foreground star velocity outliers.

evidence.quote: First, we use a Voronoi tessellation (cite: Capellari2003) to bin our MUSE data to a minimum S/N of ${\sim}35$, computed at the wavelength range of $5300{-}5500$ Å. We use then the Penalized Pixel-Fitting (pPXF) code (cite: Capellari2004; Capellari2017) to fit the spectrum of each Voronoi bin.
The stellar mass map is then reconstructed using the weights assigned by pPXF to each SSP spectrum, given that the current stellar mass of each template is known.
Finally, we have identified foreground stars as velocity outliers in the SSP fitting and we have masked those pixels for the analysis carried out in this paper.

analysis_steps.goal: Construct star formation rate surface density maps from VLT MUSE emission lines

method.value: Fit single Gaussian profiles to emission lines in each pixel, deredden Halpha using Balmer decrement, remove AGN/LINER pixels via BPT diagram, remove and spatially redistribute DIG emission using [S II]/Halpha, apply S/N cuts, and convert corrected Halpha flux to SFR.

evidence.quote: As part of the PHANGS–MUSE DAP (cite: Emsellem2021), we fit single Gaussian profiles to a number of emission lines for each pixel of the final combined MUSE mosaic of each galaxy in our sample.

Next, we remove pixels that are dominated by active galactic nuclei (AGN) or low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINER) ionization from our sample, performing a cut in the Baldwin–Phillips–Terlevich (cite: BPT) diagram

After performing this correction and removing the DIG contribution of the H$\alpha$ flux, we rescale the DIG-corrected H$\alpha$ map by 1 plus the fraction of flux removed, to keep the total H$\alpha$ flux constant.

Pixels below this S/N cut, pixels with $C_ \text{H\,\check@mathfonts\fontsize\sf@size\z@\selectfont II} \leq 0$ or pixels where $\mathrm{H}\alpha_\mathrm{obs} / \mathrm{H}\beta_\mathrm{obs} < 2.86$, are considered nondetections (see Sec. [3.2](#sec:fit)).

analysis_steps.goal: Match spatial resolution, rebin across spatial scales, correct for inclination, and apply environmental masks and detection fraction cuts

method.value: Convolve maps to common 150 pc resolution, rebin MUSE and ALMA maps to 150, 200, 300, 500, and 1000 pc pixels, apply cos(i) inclination correction, classify pixels into environments (disk, spiral arm, bar, ring, center) using Querejeta et al. (2021) masks, and restrict each environment to Sigma_* bins where both Sigma_SFR and Sigma_mol have > 60% detection fraction.

evidence.quote: To do this, we first convolve our MUSE maps to a common fixed reolution of $150$ pc, and then we rebin our $150$ pc resolution MUSE and ALMA maps to have pixel sizes of $150$ pc, $200$ pc, $300$ pc, $500$ pc and $1$ kpc.

The rebinning step is followed by an inclination correction, simply using a $\cos(i)$ multiplicative term, where $i$ is the inclination of each galaxy as listed in Table [\[tab:sample\]](#tab:sample) (cite: Lang2020).

To minimize the impact of N/Ds on our measurements, we confine our analysis only to those $\Sigma_{\star}$ ranges, where the detection fraction (of both $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ and $\Sigma_{\rm mol}$) is higher than 60%.

analysis_steps.goal: Fit the 2D star-forming plane across galactic environments using hierarchical Bayesian linear regression and compare against 1D rKS model

method.value: Center log Sigma_SFR, log Sigma_*, and log Sigma_mol by fixed full-sample means and fit log Sigma_SFR,i = C_*,i log Sigma_* + C_mol,i log Sigma_mol + C_norm using hierarchical Bayesian linear regression in PyMC3 with a single common C_norm and intrinsic scatter sigma_intr across environments. Compare 2D plane model to 1D rKS model using leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation.

In order to find the best-fitting parameters that describe the star-forming plane in each environment, as defined in Eq. [\[eq:plane_eq\]](#eq:plane_eq), we perform a Bayesian hierarchical linear regression, based on routines from the PyMC3 python package (cite: pymc3).
We compare the models using leave-one-out (cite: LOO) cross-validation, a standard model comparison method (cite: Vehtari2017).

For consistency we apply a fixed normalization to the data ($\langle \log \Sigma_{\star} \rangle = 8.11$, $\langle \log \Sigma_{\rm mol} \rangle = 7.25$ and $\langle \log \Sigma_{\rm SFR} \rangle = -2.48$) throughout this work

findings_qualitative.value: Significant variations (>1 sigma) exist in the posterior distributions of C_* and C_mol across galactic environments at 150 pc resolution, with C_* spanning negative to positive values (-0.41 in bars to 0.45 in spiral arms) and C_mol remaining positive (0.83 to 1.01).

evidence.quote: The dependence of $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ on $\Sigma_{\star}$ spans a wide range of slopes, with negative and positive values, while the dependence of $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$ on $\Sigma_{\rm mol}$ is always positive. Bars show the most negative value of $C_{\star}$ ($-0.41$), which is a sign of longer depletion times, while spiral arms show the highest $C_{\star}$ among all environments ($0.45$).

findings_qualitative.value: Environmental differences in the star-forming plane homogenize toward coarser spatial resolutions and become smaller than 1 sigma at scales larger than 300-500 pc.

evidence.quote: It shows that at spatial scales larger than $300$ pc, the differences between the posteriors of different environments become smaller than $1\sigma$ (with respect to the full-sample measurement), especially for $C_{\rm mol}$.
These variations between environments homogenize toward lower spatial resolutions. Differences are no longer significant at spatial scales larger than ${\sim}500$ pc.

findings_qualitative.value: Scatter around the star-forming plane decreases toward larger spatial scales and varies by environment at 150 pc, with centers and spiral arms showing lower scatter and disks showing larger scatter than the full sample.

evidence.quote: The first noticeable feature is how the scatter decreases toward larger spatial scales.

The figure also shows that at ${\sim}150$ pc, the scatter in certain environments is significantly lower than in others. Centers and spiral arms show a particularly low scatter, whereas disk is the only environment that shows a scatter larger than the full sample.

findings_qualitative.value: The 2D plane model is formally favored over the 1D resolved Kennicutt-Schmidt (rKS) power law at >3 sigma across all spatial scales via leave-one-out cross-validation, even though the scatter reduction is modest.

evidence.quote: Despite offering only a modest improvement in the scatter, we find that the plane model is formally favored over the rKS at all spatial scales.

The figure shows that the LOO statistic for the plane model is higher than for the rKS model at all spatial scales at the ${>}3\sigma$ level, and that the preference for the plane model becomes stronger at high spatial resolution.

findings_qualitative.value: Adopting a constant alpha_CO = 4.35 M_sun pc^-2 (K km s^-1)^-1 instead of a metallicity-dependent prescription does not qualitatively alter the environmental differences or relative predictive power of C_* and C_mol.

evidence.quote: It is easy to see that even though some specific coefficients may change, the relative difference between environments, and the relative predictive power of $C_{\star}$ and $C_{\rm mol}$ remains qualitatively the same.

claims.hypothesis: A universal 2D planar star formation relation (Sigma_SFR proportional to Sigma_*^C_* Sigma_mol^C_mol) holds across all galactic environments at 150 pc resolution if Sigma_* and Sigma_mol alone regulate local star formation.
claims.experiment: Perform hierarchical Bayesian linear regression of log Sigma_SFR as a function of log Sigma_* and log Sigma_mol at 150 pc resolution across five morphologically defined galactic environments (disk, spiral arm, bar, ring, center) in 18 PHANGS galaxies.
claims.result: Significant (>1 sigma) differences in C_* and C_mol are found across environments: C_* ranges from -0.41 +- 0.01 in bars to 0.45 +- 0.02 in spiral arms, while C_mol ranges from 0.83 +- 0.01 in bars to 1.01 +- 0.01 in rings.
claims.finding: The star-forming plane is not universal across galactic environments at 150 pc scales, implying an additional physical mechanism not captured by Sigma_* or Sigma_mol regulates star formation.

evidence.quote: If the SFR in a given region is primarily driven by these two quantities, then, this ‘star-forming plane’ should not change significantly between individual galaxies or among different galactic environments.

We found significant differences (${>}1\sigma$) in the coefficients that describe the star-forming plane across galactic environments. These differences are particularly significant for bars, spiral arms and rings. We interpret these variations as evidence for an additional regulator mechanism that is not captured by neither $\Sigma_{\star}$ nor $\Sigma_{\rm mol}$.

claims.hypothesis: Differences in the star-forming plane across galactic environments depend on spatial resolution and disappear at coarse (~kpc) scales due to blending of structures and reduced pixel counts.
claims.experiment: Rebin the 150 pc resolution MUSE and ALMA surface density maps to pixel scales of 150 pc, 200 pc, 300 pc, 500 pc, and 1 kpc and repeat the hierarchical Bayesian plane fitting at each scale.
claims.result: Differences between environmental posteriors become <1 sigma at scales larger than 300 pc for most environments and disappear above ~500 pc even for bars, while scatter decreases monotonically with increasing scale.
claims.finding: Environmental variations in the star-forming plane homogenize toward coarser spatial resolutions (>500 pc), reconciling high-resolution environmental variations with coarse-resolution surveys that find universal relations.

evidence.quote: It shows that at spatial scales larger than $300$ pc, the differences between the posteriors of different environments become smaller than $1\sigma$ (with respect to the full-sample measurement), especially for $C_{\rm mol}$.

These variations between environments homogenize toward lower spatial resolutions. Differences are no longer significant at spatial scales larger than ${\sim}500$ pc. This is because the combined effect of blending of environments at lower spatial resolutions, and the lower number of pixels per environment at large spatial scales.

claims.hypothesis: Including stellar mass surface density (a 2D plane model) provides a better prediction of Sigma_SFR than molecular gas surface density alone (the 1D rKS relation).
claims.experiment: Fit both the 2D plane model and the 1D rKS model (removing C_*) across environments and spatial scales, and compare their residual scatter and leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation statistics.
claims.result: Although adding Sigma_* does not significantly reduce the residual scatter compared to rKS, the LOO statistic favors the 2D plane model over the 1D rKS model at >3 sigma across all spatial scales, especially at high resolution.
claims.finding: The 2D plane model is formally preferred over the 1D rKS relation across all probed spatial scales, with Sigma_* providing stronger predictive value at finer spatial scales.

evidence.quote: Despite offering only a modest improvement in the scatter, we find that the plane model is formally favored over the rKS at all spatial scales.

The figure shows that the LOO statistic for the plane model is higher than for the rKS model at all spatial scales at the ${>}3\sigma$ level, and that the preference for the plane model becomes stronger at high spatial resolution.

claims.hypothesis: Variations in the star-forming plane coefficients across environments within individual galaxies are linked to local gas dynamical state, star formation efficiency, or gas fraction.
claims.experiment: For 8 galaxies hosting bars, spiral arms, and >=3 environments, correlate single-galaxy environmental C_* and C_mol coefficients against environmental averages of 13 physical and stellar population parameters.
claims.result: C_mol correlates strongly with normalized depletion time <tau / t_ff> (<rho> ~ 0.77) and Halpha velocity dispersion <sigma_Halpha> (<rho> ~ 0.72), while C_* correlates with <log SFE> (<rho> ~ 0.68) and molecular gas fraction <f_mol>.
claims.finding: Environmental variations in the star-forming plane correlate with star formation efficiency, depletion time, and gas velocity dispersion, suggesting noncircular or turbulent motions may inhibit gas collapse in environments like bars, though larger samples are needed to establish causality.

evidence.loc: What drives the environmental variations we see?
evidence.quote: Finally, we stress here that due to the relatively low number of galaxies where we can reliably probe several galactic environments (8), and since each one of the correlations has only as many points as different environments the galaxy has, we can only speculate about the influence of an additional parameter in the coefficients of the star-forming plane, rather than robustly establishing a causal relation.

We find a strong correlation of $C_{\rm mol}$ with depletion time and H$\alpha$ velocity dispersion ($\langle \rho \rangle \sim 0.77$ and $0.72$, respectively), which could be an imprint of longer depletion times driven by increased turbulent or radial motion in some galactic environments, leading to the environmental differences we observe for the star-forming plane.

why_this_data.value: The overlap of PHANGS-ALMA and PHANGS-MUSE provides high physical resolution (~150 pc) for 18 nearby (<20 Mpc), low-inclination (i < 60 deg) galaxies, making it possible to resolve the typical separation between star-forming regions, limit extinction, and isolate galactic environments.

evidence.quote: The Physics at High Angular resolution in Nearby GalaxieS (PHANGS) surveys (cite: Leroy2021b; Emsellem2021; Lee2021) provide the opportunity to explore the relation between these three quantities at a high physical resolution (${\sim}150$ pc), making it possible to isolate galactic environments and study them separately.

In order to resolve the typical separation between star-forming regions (${\sim}100$ pc), and limit the effect of extinction, the galaxies studied in this paper have been selected to have distances less than $20$ Mpc and low inclinations ($i<60^{\circ}$).

why_this_method.value: Hierarchical Bayesian linear regression represents a middle ground between treating galactic environments as completely independent or identical; rebinning rather than Gaussian convolution minimizes pixel-to-pixel covariance; a 60% detection fraction cut in Sigma_* bins avoids discretizing in 3D while minimizing bias from nondetections; a single C_norm avoids degeneracy with slopes.

evidence.quote: After beginning with matched resolution 150 pc MUSE and ALMA data, we favor this rebinning approach rather than, for example, convolution to a coarser Gaussian beam, because it minimized pixel-to-pixel covariance and yields approximately statistically independent measurements.

We choose to fit a single $C_{\rm norm}$ value for all different galactic environments to avoid degeneracies between the normalization ($C_{\rm norm}$) and the slopes of the planes ($C_{\star}$ and $C_{\rm mol}$).

The hierarchical linear regression represents the middle ground between assuming that different environments are completely independent populations, and assuming that they all are identical and described by the same model.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Binning data before fitting (as done in Pessa et al. 2021 for 1D relations) was rejected because discretizing data in higher dimensions for a 2D plane is problematic.

evidence.quote: In (cite: Pessa2021), we overcame this issue by binning the data before fitting a power law. Here we are trying to fit a 2D plane, and discretizing the data in higher dimensions becomes problematic, so we do not proceed in the same way.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Convolving to a coarser Gaussian beam to probe larger spatial scales was rejected in favor of rebinning to minimize pixel-to-pixel covariance.

evidence.quote: After beginning with matched resolution 150 pc MUSE and ALMA data, we favor this rebinning approach rather than, for example, convolution to a coarser Gaussian beam, because it minimized pixel-to-pixel covariance and yields approximately statistically independent measurements.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Exclusion of NGC 0628 from the 19 PHANGS-MUSE galaxies because its MUSE mosaic used a different observing strategy.

evidence.quote: For the sake of homogeneity of the data set, one galaxy from the PHANGS–MUSE sample (NGC 0628) has been excluded because its MUSE mosaic was obtained using a different observing strategy.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Global (full-sample) Sigma_* range cut across all environments was tested in Appendix 9 and rejected in favor of per-environment dynamic Sigma_* ranges because global truncation destabilizes spiral arm posteriors.

evidence.loc: Global versus per-environment detection fraction threshold
evidence.quote: Due to the truncation of the $\Sigma_{\star}$ range, the posterior of the spiral arms becomes unstable, and highly dependant on the threshold level applied, reaching almost a value of $C_{\rm mol}\approx1$ for a detection fraction threshold of $70\%$. Thus, we opt for a “dynamic” $\Sigma_{\star}$ range, chosen for each environment separately, as our fiducial approach.

how_they_decided_enough.value: MCMC sampling used 4 chains with 2000 iterations + 2000 burn-in and converged at R_hat ~ 1; 60% detection fraction threshold selected via sensitivity tests in Appendix 8 showing 70% drops ~22,000 more points and destabilizes posteriors.

evidence.quote: We use four Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains to sample the posterior distributions, each one of them having $2000$ iterations plus $2000$ additional burn-in iterations. The posterior is sampled using the NUTS algorithm (cite: homan2014). The convergence of the MCMC chains is ensured by using the $\hat{R} \approx 1$ criterion (cite: Gelman1992).
We also note that only $5000$ data points are lost when going from $50\%$ to $60\%$, while going from $60\%$ to $70\%$ leads to drop ${\sim}22{,}000$ additional data points.

limitations_admitted.value: At ~150 pc resolution, the lowest SFR pixels may not form enough stars to fully sample the IMF, making measured SFRs more uncertain in that regime.

evidence.quote: We acknowledge that Eq. [\[eq:sfr\]](#eq:sfr) assumes a fully sampled IMF, and that the lowest SFR pixels (especially at the ${\sim}150$ pc resolution of our data) may not form enough stars to fully sample the IMF. Hence, the measured SFR is more uncertain in this regime.

limitations_admitted.value: Spiral arm masks from Querejeta et al. (2021) were identified partially using CO emission, which may introduce selection bias toward higher gas and SFR at fixed Sigma_*.

evidence.quote: The spiral arms defined by (cite: Querejeta2021) tend to have more gas and more star formation at fixed $\Sigma_\star$. Because they were identified partially based on multiwavelength data that trace gas and SFR, this is somewhat by construction.

limitations_admitted.value: Fixing a single normalization C_norm across all environments means vertical normalization offsets between environments can be absorbed into the derived slopes C_* and C_mol.

evidence.quote: Because we keep $C_{\rm norm}$ fixed, our fitting method may allow some of the signal associated with normalization variation to the derived slopes ($C_{\star}$ and/or $C_{\rm mol}$).

limitations_admitted.value: Assuming a constant CO(2-1)-to-CO(1-0) ratio R_21 = 0.65 ignores central enhancements in R_21 (~0.18 dex), which can depress the measured C_mol slope by up to ~0.15.

evidence.loc: Star-forming plane across galactic environments at 150 pc resolution
evidence.quote: Such anticorrelation of $R_{21}$ with galactocentric radius (and thus, correlation with $\Sigma_{\rm SFR}$) implies our fiducial choice of $R_{21} = 0.65$ could potentially lead to an overestimation of the total molecular gas content in the inner and denser regions of the galaxy, and to an underestimation of the gas content in the outer regions. This can effectively depress the measured $C_{\rm mol}$ slope by up to ${\sim}0.15$.

limitations_admitted.value: Covariance between C_* and C_mol is partially an artifact of the fitting procedure and sample size.

evidence.loc: Toy model to test the hierarchical fitting
evidence.quote: Secondly, this test shows that the covariance between $C_{\star}$ and $C_{\rm mol}$ discussed in Sec. [4](#sec:results) is partially an artifact resulting from the fitting, as we recover it even though the real coefficients were chosen independently.

limitations_admitted.value: Only 8 galaxies meet the criteria for single-galaxy multi-environment correlation analysis, which is too small to establish causal relations for third parameters.

evidence.loc: What drives the environmental variations we see?
evidence.quote: Finally, we stress here that due to the relatively low number of galaxies where we can reliably probe several galactic environments (8), and since each one of the correlations has only as many points as different environments the galaxy has, we can only speculate about the influence of an additional parameter in the coefficients of the star-forming plane, rather than robustly establishing a causal relation.

referee_caveats_inferred: Forcing a single intercept C_norm across all environments while centering all variables on the global sample mean (rather than per-environment means) mathematically couples any environment-dependent offset in mean depletion time directly into the fitted slopes C_* and C_mol, particularly when an environment (e.g. bars or centers) does not sit at the global mean Sigma_*.

Applying a per-environment detection fraction cut in Sigma_* bins rather than modeling censored data (upper limits) in the Bayesian likelihood can still leave residual truncation bias near the 60% threshold.

In the single-galaxy correlation analysis (Sec. 5.2), correlating C_mol and C_* against <log SFE> and <tau / t_ff> is partially circular because SFE and tau are algebraically constructed from Sigma_SFR and Sigma_mol.
